newsitem.title: USA: FULL TEXT - Intel Corp Q4 results.
newsitem.headline: FULL TEXT - Intel Corp Q4 results.

text.p: Intel Corp Tuesday reported financial results for the fourth quarter of 1996. The following is a copy of the company's news release.

SANTA CLARA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jan. 14, 1997--Record unit shipments for Intel Corporation's Pentium(R) and Pentium(R) Pro processors lifted the company's 1996 revenue and earnings per share 29 percent and 44 percent, respectively, from 1995, the company said today. 1996 was the seventh consecutive year of both record revenue and earnings for Intel.
Revenue totaled $20.8 billion in 1996, up from $16.2 billion in 1995. Net income was $5.2 billion or $5.81 per share, up from $3.6 billion or $4.03 per share in 1995.

Fourth quarter revenue was $6.4 billion, up 41 percent from $4.6 billion for the fourth quarter of 1995. Net income was $1.9 billion for the fourth quarter, up from $867 million for the comparable period a year ago. Earnings per share in the fourth quarter rose to $2.13 from $0.98 in the final quarter of 1995, an increase of 117 percent.

"Intel hit on all cylinders in 1996, the 25th anniversary of the introduction of the microprocessor," said Dr. Andrew S. Grove, president and chief executive officer. "Fueling demand in 1996 were a number of factors including the continued growth of the Internet, the rapid penetration of PCs into emerging markets, especially in Asia, the beginnings of a corporate computing upgrade cycle and the increasing role the PC plays as a communications device. Our manufacturing performance was superb as we ramped to meet increased demand for our processors while successfully converting to 0.35 process technology."

In the fourth quarter, the company repurchased a total of 2.7 million shares of common stock at a cost of $335 million under an ongoing program. For the full year the company repurchased 16.8 million shares at a cost of $1.3 billion. Since the program began in 1990, the company has repurchased 84.9 million shares at a total cost of $3.5 billion.

During the quarter the company announced its regular quarterly cash dividend of $0.05 per share. The dividend is payable on March 1, 1997 to stockholders of record on February 1, 1997. Upon payment of this dividend, Intel will have paid a dividend for eighteen consecutive quarters.

Intel's Board of Directors approved a two-for-one stock split to be effected as a special stock distribution of one share of Common Stock for each share of the company's Common Stock outstanding, subject to stockholder approval of an increase in authorized shares at Intel's annual meeting on May 21, 1997. None of the share or per share amounts in this release have been adjusted to take into account the potential stock split.
The company also announced that a special "Thank You" bonus of $1000 per person (adjusted to reflect pay rates in countries outside the U.S.) will be paid to all employees worldwide this month.
The following statements are based on current expectations. These statements are forward looking and actual results may differ materially.
-- The company expects revenue for the first quarter of 1997 to be approximately flat with fourth quarter revenue of $6.4 billion.

-- Gross margin percentage in the first quarter of 1997 is expected to be flat to down from 63 percent in the fourth quarter. Intel's gross margin expectation for 1997 is 60 percent plus or minus a few points. The company still believes that over the long-term the gross margin percentage will be 50 percent plus or minus a few points.
-- Expenses (R& D plus MG &A) in the first quarter of 1997 are expected to be approximately 4 to 5 percent higher than the expenses of $1.2 billion in the fourth quarter of 1996.
-- The tax rate in 1997 is expected to be 35.5 percent.

-- The company expects interest and other income for the first quarter of 1997 to be approximately $130 million, assuming no significant changes in cash balances or interest rates and no unusual items.
-- Capital spending for 1997 is expected to be $4.5 billion, up from $3.0 billion in 1996. Depreciation is expected to be $2.5 billion for 1997, up from $1.9 billion in 1996.

The above statements contained in this outlook are forward-looking statements that involve a number of risks and uncertainties. In addition to factors discussed above, among other factors that could cause actual results to differ materially are the following: business conditions and growth in the computing industry and general economy; changes in customer order patterns, including timing of delivery and changes in seasonal fluctuations in PC buying patterns; competitive factors, such as rival chip architectures, competing software-compatible microprocessors, acceptance of new products and price pressures; risk of inventory obsolescence due to shifts in market demand; variations in inventory valuation;

timing of software industry product introductions; continued success in technological advances and their implementation, including the manufacturing ramp; excess or shortage of manufacturing capacity; risks associated with foreign operations; changes in the mix of microprocessor type and speeds and related motherboards; costs and yield issues associated with production at factories; litigation involving intellectual property and consumer issues; level of stock repurchases and employee stock option exercises; and other risk factors listed from time to time in the company's SEC reports, including but not limited to the report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 28, 1996 (Part I, Item 2, Outlook section).

-- Unit shipments of microprocessors and chipsets set new records during the quarter. Flash memory, embedded processors and microcontrollers were up in unit shipments but experienced pricing pressure due to general semiconductor industry conditions.
-- Fourth quarter gross margin percentage was positively affected by favorable product mix as revenue growth came primarily from processor products.

-- Motherboard units shipped in the fourth quarter were down as a percentage of Pentium processors shipped. For the Pentium Pro processor, the percentage of boards to processors was much higher than for Pentium processors, as would be expected when a new technology is introduced into the market.

Year Ended Year Ended Year Ended
-- Employment at the end of the 1996 was 48,500, up from 41,600 at the end of 1995.

-- In early January the company introduced the Pentium processor with MMX(TM) technology, the first microprocessor to incorporate Intel's new technology for improved performance on media-rich applications. The combination of MMX technology and new software will enhance a user's experience by enabling higher quality graphics, video and audio. The processor is initially offered at 166 and 200 MHz for desktop systems and 150 and 166 MHz for mobile computers.

-- The company, along with the United States Department of Energy's Sandia National Laboratory, demonstrated a parallel supercomputer sustaining over one trillion operations per second (teraflop). Using only three-fourths of the final supercomputer's planned 9,200 Pentium Pro processors the supercomputer achieved 1.06 teraflops, shattering the previous industry performance record of 368.2 gigaflops. The supercomputer is expected to be delivered to Sandia National Laboratory in the first half of 1997.

-- Intel and Microsoft announced an initiative to develop the NetPC reference platform. The NetPC is a new member of the PC family that will give organizations another tool to reduce the costs of business computing without sacrificing performance or compatibility. Networking & Communications Products

-- During the quarter a number of PC manufacturers began volume shipment of systems bundled with Intel's Video Phone with Proshare(TM) technology. Proshare technology helps bring reliable low-cost videoconferencing to home consumers over standard phone lines.

-- Intel announced a new Internet video phone that adds a new dimension to Internet communications by allowing users to talk to and see each other while using other Internet applications, such as browsing the Web, exchanging photos, or playing games. A beta version of the new Intel Internet Video Phone software is available free of charge at Intel's Connected PC Web site.

-- Intel and IBM announced a broad-based effort called the Advanced Manageability Alliance to significantly reduce the support costs of high-performance PCs in networked environments. The two companies plan to work together to define, develop, integrate and deliver standards-based solutions that enable customers to simplify the installation, configuration and management of networked PCs.

-- Intel extended and enhanced its industry leading virus protection line of products by announcing enhanced versions of both LANDesk(R) Virus Protect for Windows NT(TM) and LANDesk Virus Protect for NetWare(TM) servers, and a new product, LANDesk Virus Protect v4.0 for clients and standalone PCs.

-- Intel began shipping LANDesk Support Center, a new integrated software product that allows PC help desks to quickly resolve problems for networked PCs. The product offers built-in knowledge base technology and integrated desktop management tools that help support analysts resolve more problems on the first call, thereby reducing support costs.
-- Intel announced its new Express 10/100 Fast Ethernet Switch making it more cost-effective and easier for businesses to deploy Fast Ethernet networks.

-- Intel introduced a personal computer enhancement product, the Intel Smart Video Recorder III, that lets PC users capture and compress video from ordinary sources like VCRs and camcorders, edit it on their PCs, and then store the video to a computer disk or send it out to the Internet.

-- Intel announced the availability of a new single-chip Universal Serial Bus (USB) controller, part of an Intel led industry-wide initiative to use USB technology to make it much easier to add peripherals, such as printers, scanners and joysticks, to a PC.

-- At fall Comdex, more than 30 I2O (Intelligent I/O) SIG member companies announced I2O-ready products for enterprise computing, including Pentium and Pentium Pro processor-based servers, motherboards, adapter cards and software. The I2O architecture, led by Intel, improves server performance and enables interoperability of storage and network interfaces.

-- Intel announced it plans on delivering will deliver cryptographic technologies in hardware to enable increased levels of protection for data communicated over the Internet for business and commerce. Hewlett-Packard announced it will use this technology in its International Cryptographic Framework, which when used with Intel hardware, is currently the only U.S. government export-approved encryption framework.

-- The company announced in November it intends to build factories at two new locations, an advanced logic wafer fabrication plant in Fort Worth, Texas and an assembly/test plant in San Jose, Costa Rica. The first phase of the Fort Worth fab (Fab 16) is projected to cost $1.3 billion and is scheduled to be operational by 1999. The Costa Rican assembly/test plant is projected to cost $300 million and is scheduled to begin operations in early 1998.

-- Intel became the first major company to sign a Project XL Final Project Agreement with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Intel worked with the EPA and state and local officials to develop a five year plan to provide better environmental performance than required by the regulatory system, but with greater public accountability and lower administrative costs. The agreement with the EPA pertains to Intel's Fab 12 in Chandler, Arizona.
Q4 1996 net revenue of $6.4 billion was up 41 percent from Q4 1995, driven primarily by higher revenue from sales of Pentium and Pentium Pro processors and related board-level products, and chipsets.

Gross margin percentage in the fourth quarter was 63 percent, compared to 48 percent in the fourth quarter of 1995. The rise in the gross margin percentage was primarily the result of a more favorable product mix in Q4 1996, as the company sold more processor products as a percentage of sales than in Q4 1995. Q4 1995 results were also adversely impacted by inventory writedowns of purchased components.

Q4 1996 total expenses (R&D and MG&A) of $1.2 billion increased 35 percent from Q4 1995 expenses due primarily to higher levels of R&D, advertising and revenue dependent expenses. Expenses were 19% of revenues in Q4 1996, down from 20% in Q4 1995.
During the quarter, interest and other income was $133 million, up from $70 million in Q4 1995 due primarily to higher cash balances.

Capital spending was $790 million and depreciation was $519 million in Q4 1996. Accounts receivable increased by $235 million in the quarter. The company's average days-sales-outstanding was 45, a decrease of 5 days from the third quarter.

During Q4 1996, the company repurchased 2.7 million shares of common stock at a cost of $335 million under an ongoing program. As of December 28, 1996 the company's potential put warrant obligation was $275 million to buy back 4.5 million shares of common stock. Of the total 110 million shares authorized for repurchase, approximately 84.9 million shares have been repurchased and 20.6 million shares of common stock remain available for repurchase under the stock repurchase program, after reserving for 4.5 million shares to cover outstanding put warrants.

Two-for-one stock split to be effected as a special stock distribution

The Board of Directors' declaration of a special stock distribution (the "stock split") is subject to the condition that the stockholders approve an increase in total authorized common shares from the current limit of 1.4 billion shares to 4.5 billion. Intel's stockholders will vote on the increase at the company's annual meeting on May 21, 1997, as will be more fully described in Intel's proxy material to be distributed at a later date. The stock split would be declared shortly thereafter. The declaration and amount of any future cash dividend is subject to the discretion of the Board of Directors.

The company's 1998 Step-Up Warrants also would be adjusted to reflect the stock split. 1998 Step-Up Warrant holders would receive one additional warrant for each warrant they currently hold, and the exercise price of the warrants would be adjusted to reflect the stock split. Following the adjustment, each outstanding 1998 Step-Up Warrant would entitle the holder to buy one share of Intel Common Stock at one-half of the per-share prices specified in the May 5, 1995 Notice to Warrant Holders. The warrant distribution would take place at the same time as the stock distribution and is similarly subject to the condition that the stockholders approve the increase in authorized shares at the company's annual meeting.
The record and payment dates will be announced later.
